issue.title: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite: GetValues rejects an array shorter than the row, unlike the IDataRecord contract
issue.body:
`SqliteDataReader.GetValues` throws when the array is shorter than the row, where the `IDataRecord` contract says it copies what fits. (Split out of #39343 so each change can be reviewed on its own.)

### What the documentation says

[IDataRecord.GetValues](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.data.idatarecord.getvalues), Remarks:

> You can pass an Object array that contains fewer than the number of columns that are contained in the resulting row. Only the amount of data the Object array holds is copied to the array.

### Why this is a bug

The contract explicitly allows a short array and says what happens: the first `values.Length` columns are copied and that count is returned. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` instead, so code that reads only the leading columns of a wide row into a fixed-size buffer (valid against SqlClient, Npgsql and MySqlConnector) fails here.

```csharp
using var reader = connection.ExecuteReader("SELECT 1, 2, 3");
reader.Read();
reader.GetValues(new object[2]);   // IndexOutOfRangeException; documented: copies 2 values, returns 2
```

The current behaviour is pinned by `GetValues_throws_when_too_narrow`. I have a small change that follows the documented contract (copy `Math.Min(values.Length, FieldCount)` values and return that count) and replaces that test; I'll link it here.

Found with https://github.com/pengdows/pengdows.AdoNetApiTest.conformance

issue.title: DbContextPool not decrementing active_dbcontexts metrics when overloaded
issue.body:
### Bug description

I want to use the DbContext pool. Because I have a few places where it's up to the developer to properly dispose the DbContext I want to monitor pool usage and context disposal.

There are no metrics for the pool (e.g. rented out db contexts), so I tried monitoring the 'microsoft.entityframeworkcore.active_dbcontexts' metric. However I notice that this metric is not correct when used in combination with a pool.

I know that the metric includes the idle contexts in the pool as discussed in https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/35855 , but whenever the pool is exhausted and falls back to creating new contexts, those contexts are also not decremented from the metric after disposal, so you get an ever-incrementing metric.

A project to reproduce and show this error can be found [here](https://github.com/gijs-hendrikx/DbContextPool_Debugger).

The project demonstrates the following:
* A pool of 20 db contexts
* Every 30 seconds: rent out 25 db contexts at once and dispose them all afterwards

issue.title: GroupBy with Any() or All() prevents aggregates over reference navigations from being lifted into a join
issue.body:
### Bug description


In EF Core 11, `GroupBy(key).Select(g => g.Max(o => o.Nav.Property))` now translates to a single `SELECT` with a join (#27933, fixed by #38668). Adding an `Any()` or `All()` call anywhere in the same result selector disables that optimisation for *every* aggregate in the group, and the query falls back to a correlated sub-query per aggregate, as EF Core 10 did.

`Any` and `All` themselves translate to a correlated `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS`, which is reasonable. The problem is that their presence also demotes their siblings: aggregates that read a reference navigation stop being lifted into the shared join and each become their own correlated sub-query.

```csharp
db.Orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        g.Key,
        Region = g.Max(o => o.Customer.Region),
        Amount = g.Sum(o => o.Amount),
        Westerly = g.Count(o => o.Customer.Region == "West"),
    });
```

Produces:

```sql
SELECT [o].[CustomerId] AS [Key], MAX([c].[Region]) AS [Region], COALESCE(SUM([o].[Amount]), 0.0) AS [Amount], COUNT(CASE
    WHEN [c].[Region] = N'West' THEN 1
```

issue.title: Precompiled query generation emits expression variable names verbatim, producing invalid C# for names that are not identifiers
issue.body:
### Bug description

`LinqToCSharpSyntaxTranslator` turns EF's shaper expression trees into C# for precompiled queries. Block variables and lambda parameters keep the names they were given when the expression tree was built. The translator uniquifies those names (`UniquifyVariableName`) but does not check that they are valid identifiers, and emits them directly (`VariableDeclarator(Identifier(name))`).

Expression tree variable names are arbitrary strings. In the relational shaper some are derived from model configuration: the JSON materializer names runtime constants after JSON property names (already sanitized by `PrecompiledQueryCodeGenerator.SanitizeIdentifierName`, see `Invalid_identifier_json_property_name`), and any block variable named the same way is emitted unsanitized. During review of #39014, a block variable named `<jsonPropertyName>Read` for a complex collection whose JSON name was `1!NOT VALID COLLECTION;` produced:

```
Test.EFInterceptors.InvalidNameContext.g.cs(127,26): error CS1001: Identifier expected
```

That PR avoided the problem by leaving the variable unnamed, but the translator remains one named variable away from the same failure.

### Expected behavior

Any variable or parameter name the translator emits is a valid C# identifier, the same way runtime constant names already are (`1!NOT VALID;` becomes `_1_NOT_VALID_`).

### Proposed fix

Move the identifier sanitizer from `PrecompiledQueryCodeGenerator` into `LinqToCSharpSyntaxTranslator` as a shared method and apply it in `UniquifyVariableName`, which every emitted variable and lambda parameter name already passes through. The generator calls the shared method for runtime constants. One translator unit test:

```csharp
var i = Parameter(typeof(int), "1!not valid;");
AssertStatement(Block(variables: [i], Assign(i, Constant(3))), """
{
    var _1_not_valid_ = 3;
}
""");
```

Allow changing CLR type in query translation without additional SQL
issue.body:
In some rare cases, during query translation we want to change the CLR type, but without an actual SQL conversion being necessary. For example, if an enum that's value-converted to string has ToString() called on it, nothing needs to be done in SQL (the database value is already a string), but in the query tree we need to switch from the enum type to string.

Ideally we'd be able to simply replace the enum-typed node with an identical string-typed node - but there's no reliable way to change all node types (column, function call...), unless we introduce e.g. an abstract WithType() to SqlExpression.

The alternative way would be to add a special conversion node - which would extend SqlExpression - but to simply skip it in SQL generation. The disadvantage here is that any sort of pattern matching on the node would fail (e.g. is this node a column?).

In the meantime, we'd applying a SQL conversion, which should be a no-op.

issue.title: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite: disposing a SqliteCommand closes its open SqliteDataReader
issue.body:
### Bug description

Disposing a `SqliteCommand` while a reader it returned is still open closes that reader, so the next `Read` throws:

```
System.InvalidOperationException: Invalid attempt to call Read when reader is closed.
```

`SqliteCommand.Dispose(bool)` calls `DisposePreparedStatements`, which disposes `DataReader` before finalizing the statements the reader is stepping through.

Code that returns a reader from a method and disposes the command on the way out (a common data-access-layer pattern) works with SqlClient, Npgsql and System.Data.SQLite, but fails with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite. We found this while building an ADO.NET conformance suite; every Microsoft.Data.Sqlite version we tried (2.2.6 through 10.0.13 and 11.0.0-rc.2) behaves this way.

### Your code

```csharp
using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
connection.Open();
var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT 42";
using var reader = command.ExecuteReader();
command.Dispose();

reader.Read(); // InvalidOperationException: Invalid attempt to call Read when reader is closed.
```

### Proposed fix

When the command is disposed with an open reader, finish the disposal (finalize the statements, raise `Disposed`) when the reader closes. Closing the connection still closes the reader and disposes the command. A PR follows.

### Microsoft.Data.Sqlite version

10.0.13; also 11.0.0-rc.2.26504.105

### Target framework

.NET 10.0

Linux

issue.body:
Reverse engineering a SQLite database that has an index on an expression fails with an `InvalidOperationException` instead of skipping the index (with a warning) or scaffolding the rest of the model.

### Repro

```sql
CREATE TABLE T (Id integer PRIMARY KEY, Name text);
CREATE INDEX IX_T_lower ON T (lower(Name));
```

```
dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold "Data Source=repro.db" Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite
```

### Actual

```
System.InvalidOperationException: The data is NULL at ordinal 0. This method can't be called on NULL values. Check using IsDBNull before calling.
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteValueReader.GetString(Int32 ordinal)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Scaffolding.Internal.SqliteDatabaseModelFactory.GetIndexes(DbConnection connection, DatabaseTable table)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Scaffolding.Internal.SqliteDatabaseModelFactory.GetTables(...)
```

`GetIndexes` reads the key columns with:

```sql
SELECT "name", "desc"
FROM pragma_index_xinfo(@index)
WHERE key = 1
ORDER BY "seqno"
```

For an expression column SQLite returns `cid = -2` and `name = NULL`, and the code then calls `reader2.GetString(0)` on it:

```
seqno  cid  name  desc  key
0      -2   NULL  0     1
```

The same applies to expression columns mixed with real columns, e.g. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IX ON T (Name, (Name || 'x'))`.

### Expected

Scaffolding completes. Expression indexes can't be represented in the model (see #28360), so the index should be skipped, ideally with a warning similar to the one used for indexes over columns that can't be scaffolded.

### Notes

- Found while working on #11298; not related to that fix.
- This is in `SqliteDatabaseModelFactory.GetIndexes`, where `Check.DebugAssert(column != null, ...)` follows the lookup, so the NULL name isn't anticipated.

issue.title: EF Core 7 GroupBy with Owned Entity perf Regression
issue.body:
EF Core 7 for SQL Server has a SQL query translation regression from EF Core 6 for GroupBy with aggregate functions.

For the query:

```
var query = context.Items
    .GroupBy(x => x.Group)
    .Select(x => new
    {
        Set1Value1 = x.Sum(v => v.Set1.Value1),
        Set1Value2 = x.Sum(v => v.Set1.Value2),
        Set2Value1 = x.Sum(v => v.Set2.Value1),
        Set2Value2 = x.Sum(v => v.Set2.Value2),
    });

```
SQL generated from EF Core 6:

```
SELECT COALESCE(SUM([i].[Set1_Value1]), 0) AS [Set1Value1], COALESCE(SUM([i].[Set1_Value2]), 0) AS [Set1Value2], COALESCE(SUM([i].[Set2_Value1]), 0) AS [Set2Value1], COALESCE(SUM([i].[Set2_Value2]), 0) AS [Set2Value2]
FROM [Items] AS [i]
GROUP BY [i].[Group]
```

SQL generated from EF Core 7.0.0

```
SELECT (
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM([i0].[Set1_Value1]), 0)
    FROM [Items] AS [i0]
    WHERE [i].[Group] = [i0].[Group] OR (([i].[Group] IS NULL) AND ([i0].[Group] IS NULL))) AS [Set1Value1], (
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM([i1].[Set1_Value2]), 0)
    FROM [Items] AS [i1]
    WHERE [i].[Group] = [i1].[Group] OR (([i].[Group] IS NULL) AND ([i1].[Group] IS NULL))) AS [Set1Value2], (
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM([i2].[Set2_Value1]), 0)
    FROM [Items] AS [i2]
    WHERE [i].[Group] = [i2].[Group] OR (([i].[Group] IS NULL) AND ([i2].[Group] IS NULL))) AS [Set2Value1], (
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM([i3].[Set2_Value2]), 0)
    FROM [Items] AS [i3]
    WHERE [i].[Group] = [i3].[Group] OR (([i].[Group] IS NULL) AND ([i3].[Group] IS NULL))) AS [Set2Value2]
FROM [Items] AS [i]
GROUP BY [i].[Group]
```
 
EF Core 7 is now adding sub queries to the SELECT for each of the SUM functions.  I believe that the EF Core 6 SQL is better and more efficient. 

I have created a repo https://github.com/martosource/EfCoreGroupByOwnedTest

issue.title: Migrator retains every pending migration's target model for the whole Migrate call
issue.body:
`Migrator.PopulateMigrations` puts the pending migrations into a list that is held for the entire `Migrate` run, and `Migration.TargetModel` caches the built (and then runtime-initialized) model on each instance. So on a fresh database with N migrations over a large model, peak memory is roughly N × model size.

**Measured:** 174 migrations over a model of about 200 tables. Peak memory was 1,033 MiB, and under a 1 GiB container limit the run threw `OutOfMemoryException` after 165 migrations. Overriding `Migration.TargetModel` so the model is not cached brought the peak down to 295 MiB, with an identical resulting schema.

**Suggestion:** stop caching `_targetModel`, or create migrations lazily in `GetMigrationCommandLists`, so each model can be collected once its SQL has been generated.

**Repro:** any project with about 150 migrations over a model of about 200 entities. Run `Database.Migrate()` against an empty database under `docker run --memory 1g`.

**Versions:** Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore 11.0.0-rc.2.26504.105, Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL 11.0.0-rc.2, .NET 11.0.0-rc.2 runtime.

**Related:** #34276 and #18620 (make BuildTargetModel optional), #19710 (stream migration commands).

### What problem are you trying to solve?

Following up on https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/35863#issuecomment-6532548519 and #39485, there are several remaining places in JSON materialization that still throw the generic `CoreStrings.JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` (`"Invalid token type: '{tokenType}'."`) without context about what was expected or which type/property was being materialized:

1. **`IncludeJsonEntityCollection` (top-level JSON collections)**:
   - Unlike `MaterializeJsonEntityCollection` (updated in #39485), `IncludeJsonEntityCollection` does not currently receive `IPropertyBase structuralProperty`, so a `null` or non-object element in a top-level JSON collection still throws `Invalid token type: 'Null'` instead of `JsonEntityCollectionNullElement` / `JsonEntityCollectionExpectedObject`.
2. **Root token mismatches in relational JSON shaper methods**:
   - `MaterializeJsonStructuralType`, `MaterializeJsonNullableValueStructuralType`, and `IncludeJsonEntityReference` throw `JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` when the root token is not `StartObject` (e.g., when a JSON array is stored where a JSON object is expected).
   - `MaterializeJsonEntityCollection` and `IncludeJsonEntityCollection` throw `JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` when the root token is not `StartArray` (e.g., when a JSON object is stored where a JSON array is expected).
3. **Stale `tokenType` passed when checking for `EndObject` in `MaterializeJsonEntityCollection` and `IncludeJsonEntityCollection`**:
   - After invoking `innerShaper`, both methods check `if (manager.CurrentReader.TokenType != JsonTokenType.EndObject)` but pass `tokenType.ToString()` (which is still `StartObject`) instead of `manager.CurrentReader.TokenType.ToString()`.
4. **Primitive collection `JsonValueReaderWriter`s (`JsonCollectionOfStructsReaderWriter`, `JsonCollectionOfNullableStructsReaderWriter`, `JsonCollectionOfReferencesReaderWriter`)**:
   - Throw `JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` when the outer value is not `StartArray` or when an element token is invalid for the element type, without indicating what token/value was expected.

### Describe the solution you'd like

1. Pass `IPropertyBase structuralProperty` (or the declaring type and property names) to `IncludeJsonEntityCollection` so that top-level JSON collections throw the same `JsonEntityCollectionNullElement` and `JsonEntityCollectionExpectedObject` exceptions as `MaterializeJsonEntityCollection`.
2. Replace or enhance the root-level `JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` throws in JSON shaper methods so they name the structural type / property and state whether a JSON object or JSON array was expected.
3. Fix the `EndObject` check in `MaterializeJsonEntityCollection` and `IncludeJsonEntityCollection` to report `manager.CurrentReader.TokenType` instead of the stale `tokenType`.
4. Include the expected token/value context in `JsonReaderInvalidTokenType` (or dedicated resource strings) for primitive collection `JsonValueReaderWriter`s.

issue.title: SqliteCommand falsely reports bound prefix-less parameters as unbound when another parameter is missing
issue.body:
### Bug description

When executing a command where a parameter was added without prefix (for example `command.Parameters.AddWithValue("Parameter", 1)`), Microsoft.Data.Sqlite successfully binds it to `@Parameter`, `$Parameter`, or `:Parameter` via `SqliteParameter.FindPrefixedParameter`.

However, if another parameter in the query is missing or unset, `SqliteCommand.GetStatements()` checks which parameters are unbound by doing:
```csharp
if (_parameters != null && !_parameters.Cast<SqliteParameter>().Any(p => p.ParameterName == name))
{
    unboundParams.Add(name);
}
```

Because `name` from SQLite is prefixed (e.g. `@Parameter`) while `p.ParameterName` is `Parameter`, `p.ParameterName == name` evaluates to false. As a result, the already-bound parameter is incorrectly included in `unboundParams`, and the exception message reports it as unbound:

```
System.InvalidOperationException: SQLite Error 1: 'SqliteCommand.Prepare' requires all parameters to be bound. The following parameters are unbound: @Parameter, @Parameter2
```

In addition:
1. When `_parameters` was never accessed on the command (`_parameters == null`), `unboundParams` is never populated, resulting in an empty missing parameters list (`Must add values for the following parameters: `).
2. When a query contains positional/unnamed parameters (`?`), `sqlite3_bind_parameter_name` returns null, adding null to `unboundParams` and formatting as empty strings or dangling commas.

### Your code

```csharp
using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
connection.Open();

using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT @Parameter, @Parameter2;";
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("Parameter", 1); // Bound successfully, but reported as unbound

command.ExecuteScalar();
// Throws InvalidOperationException:
// Expected: "Must add values for the following parameters: @Parameter2"
// Actual: "Must add values for the following parameters: @Parameter, @Parameter2"
```

### Stack traces

```text
System.InvalidOperationException: SQLite Error 1: 'SqliteCommand.Prepare' requires all parameters to be bound. The following parameters are unbound: @Parameter, @Parameter2
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.GetStatements()
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.ExecuteReader(CommandBehavior behavior)
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.ExecuteScalar()
```

10.0.0 / main

### Target framework

.NET 10.0 / .NET 12.0

### Operating system

Windows 11

issue.title: [M.D.Sqlite] improve support for GetSchema()
issue.body:
ADO.NET has a weakly-typed introspection API, where users can call DbConnection.GetSchema() and get information about the database (and the driver). This API is lacking in various ways - it's weakly typed and support varies across providers - but it's the only semi-standard thing, and there seems to be at least some sort of common denominator that's implemented across provider. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite currently doesn't support this - we can consider implementing a more support here to align with other ADO.NET providers.

/cc @bricelam (I know you hate GetSchema() - as do I - but that's what we have...)

issue.title: IDbCommandInterceptor.CommandFailed does not capture all command exceptions
issue.body:
## Context

When using EF Core together with Sql Server, we catch exceptions from the database (mostly `SqlException`s) and convert them to domain-specific custom exceptions.  Originally we were doing this as a `try`/`catch` inside an override of `SaveChangesAsync` in our `DbContext`.

This approach worked fine for most cases, however when we execute a stored procedure via a call like `DbContext.Database.ExecuteSqlInterpolatedAsync`, it does not use `SaveChangesAsync`, and so exceptions were not being converted in those cases.

In an attempt to create one encapsulated thing that handles the exception handling, I implemented an `IDbCommandInterceptor` using the `CommandFailed` and `CommandFailedAsync` methods.

This appeared to work as we wanted and handled regular calls (made via `SaveChangesAsync`) and stored procedure calls (and other ad-hoc calls) made via `DbContext.Database`.

However, we've come across an edge case where the `IDbCommandInterceptor` approach is not working.

- When changes to multiple entities have been made and then `SaveChangesAsync` is called, EF can decide to make some optimisations. This includes executing a batch of statements in a single database call (which makes sense to do).
- When it does this, it appears that if the first statement of the batch causes an exception, then everything works as expected - the call fails and the exception is passed to the `CommandFailedAsync` of the interceptor.
- However, if the first statement succeeds and returns a result set (such as a new timestamp version column value), but then one of the subsequent statements throws an exception, then the `CommandFailedAsync` of the interceptor is *not* called. 
  - The end result is still an exception coming from `DbContext.SaveChangesAsync`, it just isn't captured into `CommandFailedAsync`.

After debugging into the code, it appears that this is because:
- the batch statement is being executing as a Db Reader (which makes sense)
- the result `DbDataReader` is only fully processed (via calling `DbDataReader.NextResultAsync`) _after_ the handling for the interceptor is already passed. (`NextResultAsync` is called in `AffectedCountModificationCommandBatch.cs` in the `ConsumeAsync` method)

(Note: I found this blog post helpful in getting to this understanding: https://www.dbdelta.com/the-curious-case-of-undetected-sql-exceptions/)

## My Question

After all the context, my question is:

Is this expected behaviour?  

After looking at what the code is doing, it makes sense that in its current form that it behaves this way, but when I was [reading about interceptors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/logging-events-diagnostics/interceptors) I had the impression that _all_ command exceptions would be captured into the CommandFailed methods.

If it is intended to work this way, perhaps some additional documentation in the Interceptors page explaining that not all exceptions will be captured would help?

But ideally of course, it would be great if interceptors could be updated/enhanced so that an exception that appears as part of processing the `DbDataReader` would also be caught.

## Issue Reproduction code

As this involves both C# code and Sql Server code and to convince EF that it needs to use its batch command optimisation, this would be quite difficult to create a reproduction for.  However, hopefully the explanation above makes sense and is straight-forward to understand.

## Existing Issues Raised

None found on this topic.

## Work-around

In order to get the behaviour we're after, we have changed our code to have handlers in both the interceptor and within our override of `SaveChangesAsync`.  This was not a difficult change to make (if a little less neat) but we've only just found out, with a bunch of debugging, that we needed this change and why.

## Alternative Work-around not used

An alternative that was considered was to process the `DbDataReader` within the `ReaderExecutedAsync` similar to what is described within [this issue](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/31991).  

However this involves reading the entire results of every query into memory, which could defeat the purpose of using a reader for large results sets, and it has more risk of inadvertently affecting some other part of how EF works. Another minor point is that `DataTable.Load` does not support async calls, so more custom code would be required to implement that.

Target framework: `net8.0`

issue.title: Temporal query runs as a cached plain AsNoTracking query of the same shape
issue.body:
### Bug description

If a plain `AsNoTracking()` query of the same shape has already been compiled, `TemporalAll()` (and the other temporal operators) can return current rows instead of history, with no error. The temporal query picks up the cached plain query and runs it, so the generated SQL has no `FOR SYSTEM_TIME` clause. On a table that isn't temporal, SQL Server doesn't refuse the query either.

Cause: the compiled-query cache compares keys with `ExpressionEqualityComparer`, which calls `left.Equals(right)` for extension nodes. `EntityQueryRootExpression.Equals` accepts any `EntityQueryRootExpression` of the same entity type, including derived roots. `TemporalAllQueryRootExpression` returns the same hash code as its base. So when the stored key is the plain root, it says it equals the temporal root being looked up. The comparison is asymmetric: `TemporalAllQueryRootExpression.Equals` only accepts its own type.

A temporal query that runs before the plain one isn't affected, and neither is a tracked plain query: the shapes differ, because temporal operators make the query no-tracking.

Repro: https://github.com/NoahSurprenant/ef-temporal-notracking-cache-repro

I'd like to send a fix: make `EntityQueryRootExpression.Equals` require the same runtime type (`obj.GetType() == GetType()`). It comes with a unit test in `ExpressionEqualityComparerTest` and a SQL Server test in `TemporalTableSqlServerTest`. Both fail before the change and pass after it.

### Your code

```csharp
var current = await context.Blogs.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync();   // compiled and cached
var history = await context.Blogs.TemporalAll().ToListAsync();     // served from the cached plain query
// history contains only the current rows; SQL has no FOR SYSTEM_TIME ALL
```

10.0.14 (also reproduces on main)

Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer

### Target framework

.NET 10.0

Linux

N/A

issue.title: [Regression 9.0 → 10.0] Query filter with inline array of navigation columns generates SQL referencing pruned columns
issue.body:
<!--
Brouillon prêt à poster sur https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/new
Ne pas publier sans confirmation explicite.

Title (séparé du body sur GitHub) :
[Regression 9.0 → 10.0] Query filter with inline array of navigation columns generates SQL referencing pruned columns
-->

### Bug description

On EF Core 10, a global query filter that reads a navigation column via an **inline array** +
`.Any(...)` produces invalid SQL: the join-derived table for that navigation projects only the join
key (`Id`), while the filter's `EXISTS` clause still references another column from it (`ServiceId`).

**Regression:** same code works on EF Core 9.x (tested with 9.0.18 on net10.0), fails on EF Core
10.0.0–10.0.10. Also reproduced on PostgreSQL and MySQL (same error shape). Not caused by named
query filters — classic `HasQueryFilter(lambda)` reproduces it.

**Expected:** query returns `["ok"]`.

**Workaround (EF10):** avoid the inline collection — `Scope.AuthorizedServiceIds.Contains(c.Parent.ServiceId)` works.

**Likely root cause** (source reading on v10.0.10, `SqlTreePruner.PruneValues`): the inline array
becomes a `ValuesExpression` whose row value is a `ColumnExpression` (`p0.ServiceId`). EF10's
`PruneValues` ([#36159](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/pull/36159)) copies row values without
`Visit()`, so embedded column refs are never registered → join subquery pruned to `Id` only.
Related: [#34954](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/34954) (same territory, different failure).

**Runnable projects** (`dotnet run`, logs SQL):
- [EF Core 10 / net10.0 — fails](https://gist.github.com/yvesleguennec/108a935ffcf35064c01a58a118004a8f)
- [EF Core 9.0.18 / net10.0 — works](https://gist.github.com/yvesleguennec/980020be80430be47ad5fae4e5319b51)

### Your code

```csharp
public class Parent
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public int ServiceId { get; set; }
}

public class Child
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public int ParentId { get; set; }
    public Parent Parent { get; set; } = null!;
    public string Label { get; set; } = "";
}

public static class Scope
{
    public static List<int> AuthorizedServiceIds { get; set; } = [];
}

public class ReproContext(DbContextOptions<ReproContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
    public DbSet<Parent> Parents => Set<Parent>();
    public DbSet<Child> Children => Set<Child>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        modelBuilder.Entity<Parent>().HasQueryFilter(
            p => Scope.AuthorizedServiceIds.Contains(p.ServiceId));

        // Inline array of a navigation column — this is the trigger.
        modelBuilder.Entity<Child>().HasQueryFilter(c =>
            new int?[] { c.Parent.ServiceId }
                .Any(id => id.HasValue && Scope.AuthorizedServiceIds.Contains(id.Value)));
    }
}

Scope.AuthorizedServiceIds = [10];
// Seed: Parent { Id = 1, ServiceId = 10 }, Child { ParentId = 1, Label = "ok" }
var results = await context.Children.AsNoTracking().Select(c => c.Label).ToListAsync(); // throws
```

### Stack traces

```text
Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteException (0x80004005): SQLite Error 1: 'no such column: p0.ServiceId'.
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteException.ThrowExceptionForRC(Int32 rc, sqlite3 db)
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.PrepareAndEnumerateStatements()+MoveNext()
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.GetStatements()+MoveNext()
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteDataReader.NextResult()
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.ExecuteReader(CommandBehavior behavior)
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.ExecuteReaderAsync(CommandBehavior behavior, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteCommand.ExecuteDbDataReaderAsync(CommandBehavior behavior, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Storage.RelationalCommand.ExecuteReaderAsync(RelationalCommandParameterObject parameterObject, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Storage.RelationalCommand.ExecuteReaderAsync(RelationalCommandParameterObject parameterObject, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Query.Internal.SingleQueryingEnumerable`1.AsyncEnumerator.InitializeReaderAsync(AsyncEnumerator enumerator, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Query.Internal.SingleQueryingEnumerable`1.AsyncEnumerator.MoveNextAsync()
```

Same shape on PostgreSQL (`column p0.ServiceId does not exist`) and MySQL (`Unknown column 'p0.ServiceId'`).

### Verbose output

EF Core 10 — failing SQL (SQLite):

```sql
SELECT "c"."Label"
FROM "Children" AS "c"
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT "p"."Id"
    FROM "Parents" AS "p"
    WHERE "p"."ServiceId" = 10
) AS "p0" ON "c"."ParentId" = "p0"."Id"
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM (SELECT "p0"."ServiceId" AS "Value") AS "v"
    WHERE "v"."Value" = 10)
```

`p0` projects only `Id`, but the `EXISTS` still reads `p0.ServiceId`.

EF Core 9.0.18 — same code, working SQL (SQLite):

```sql
SELECT "c"."Label"
FROM "Children" AS "c"
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT "p"."Id", "p"."ServiceId"
    FROM "Parents" AS "p"
    WHERE "p"."ServiceId" = 10
) AS "p0" ON "c"."ParentId" = "p0"."Id"
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM (SELECT "p0"."ServiceId" AS "Value") AS "v"
    WHERE "v"."Value" = 10)
```

Console output (EF10): `FAIL — SqliteException: SQLite Error 1: 'no such column: p0.ServiceId'.`  
Console output (EF9): `OK — ok`

### EF Core version

10.0.10 (appeared in 10.0.0)

### Database provider

Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite 10.0.10 (primary repro above).

Also reproduced on Npgsql 10.0.0 (PostgreSQL) and Microting.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql 10.0.10 (MySQL).

### Target framework

net10.0

### Operating system

Linux (Ubuntu)

### IDE

_No response_

issue.body:
We currently translate the following LINQ query:

```c#
_ = ctx.Blogs
    .GroupBy(b => b.Id)
    .Select(g => new { g.Key, Count = g.Select(x => x.Name).Count(n => n != null) })
    .ToList();
```

... to:

```sql
SELECT [b].[Id] AS [Key], COUNT(CASE
    WHEN [b].[Name] IS NOT NULL THEN 1
END) AS [Count]
FROM [Blogs] AS [b]
GROUP BY [b].[Id]
```

... when we could just translate to:

```sql
SELECT [b].[Id] AS [Key], COUNT([b].[Name]) AS [Count]
FROM [Blogs] AS [b]
GROUP BY [b].[Id]
```

... since `COUNT(x)` only counts non-null values. This may have a perf impact (index usage).

Related to #26938
